note: E9 (Brad pt 13). An external interconnect-agreement / SLA artefact for the Meridian(transport, X) <-> Cascade(IP, Y) seam. Each clause states, in operational terms, who OWNS / REALISES / MEASURES a shared field -- the authority is to be DERIVED from the clause, not read off a label. Deliberate difficulty: the committed-rate clause names transport's carriage duty AND the IP-side ownership (the 'transport claims everything it carries' lure); the demarcation clause is written as genuinely JOINT (the correct answer is to defer to 'shared', not invent a single owner). Clauses are faithful to pragmatics.json (the gold), but the mapping from clause to X/Y/shared requires reading.

clauses.text: One-way latency is a property of the optical path and is measured and guaranteed by Meridian at the transport demarcation per the path-engineering record. Cascade specifies only the latency TIER its service requires; it does not measure or realise the delivered figure.
Path protection is realised by Meridian's diversely-routed transport and its protection switching. Cascade requires that the circuit be protected but does not operate or own the protection mechanism.

Forwarding class and scheduling priority are configured in the Cascade IP routers according to the customer's QoS policy. Meridian's optical line 'grade' is a separate transport-line classification and confers no authority over the IP service class.

The committed information rate is the customer's contracted service bandwidth under the Cascade service SLA; it is owned, set and policed by Cascade. Meridian shall provision transport capacity sufficient to CARRY the committed rate, but carriage does not confer ownership: the committed rate is a Cascade commitment, not a Meridian transport parameter.

The interconnect demarcation point and its attachment parameters are JOINTLY defined by Meridian and Cascade. Neither party's local naming governs; the demarcation is co-owned and any change requires bilateral agreement and sign-off by both parties.
